pairing: SCAN-12: the founder's age-ladder - (1) under-13 after-school + summer programs vs (2) 13-18 youth-tribe alternatives funded by stipends + program funding + transportation; what does the literature say about age-differentiated youth-program effects on crime?

entries.authors: Heller SB
entries.title: Summer jobs reduce violence among disadvantaged youth.
entries.key_finding: RCT, 1,634 disadvantaged Chicago high-school youth (13-18 band): assignment to an 8-week summer job + 25h/wk program cut violent-crime arrests 43% over 55 weeks; effect concentrated in the program+post summer window and driven by non-violent weapon/property 'other violent' categories, not drug arrests.
entries.novelty_verdict: VERIFIED (canon anchor for the HIGH-SCHOOL arc causal effect)

entries.authors: Kessler J, Tahamont S, Gelber A, Isen A
entries.title: The Effects of Youth Employment on Crime: Evidence from New York City Lotteries
entries.key_finding: NYC SYEP lottery designs extended to crime endpoints: summer youth employment reduces criminal-justice contact among low-income applicants; the jobs-crime causal channel generalizes beyond the Chicago flagship RCT.
entries.novelty_verdict: VERIFIED (secondhand-recorded: abstract not populated; NYC replication claim needs full-text check)
entries.confidence: medium (secondhand: abstract not populated in loaded routes)

entries.authors: Leos-Urbel J
entries.title: What Is a Summer Job Worth? The Impact of Summer Youth Employment on Academic Outcomes
entries.venue: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
entries.key_finding: NYC SYEP lottery (36,550 applicants, 2007): small increases in next-year school attendance among low-income high-school students - the academic-side channel adjacent to the crime mechanism (occupying unstructured time).
entries.effect_size: small attendance increases (estimates in full text)

entries.authors: Modestino AS, Paulsen R
entries.title: School's Out: How Summer Youth Employment Programs Impact Academic Outcomes
entries.key_finding: Boston SYEP experimental evidence: summer jobs raise academic outcomes for disadvantaged high-school youth; replication platform for the summer-jobs mechanism outside Chicago.

entries.authors: Bertrand M, Repka M
entries.title: One Summer Chicago PLUS: Scaling and 'Unpacking' a Successful Program
entries.key_finding: Documents scaling mechanics of the flagship summer-jobs-plus program - which component (job, mentorship, hours) carries the crime effect remains unresolved at scale.
entries.confidence: high (secondhand: abstract not populated in loaded routes)

entries.authors: Bhatt MP, Heller SB, Kapustin M et al.
entries.title: Predicting and Preventing Gun Violence: An Experimental Evaluation of READI Chicago.
entries.key_finding: RCT, N=2,456 highest-risk young men: 18-month transitional jobs + CBT. Primary serious-violence index change null after 20 months, but shooting/homicide arrests down ~1/3 in treatment group; supports jobs as mechanism for the tail (18-24) too.
entries.novelty_verdict: EXTENDED (risk-targeted extension of the jobs-crime canon; mixed result honestly reported)
entries.effect_size: no significant primary-index change; shooting/homicide arrest reduction ~1/3 (secondary)

entries.authors: Stacy C, Teles D, Gonzalez J, Walker F, Morgan J et al.
entries.title: Cash Transfers and After-School Programs: A Randomized Controlled Trial for Young Men at Risk of Violence Exposure
entries.key_finding: RCT for young men 14-17 (the exact 13-18 band) in low-income high-crime neighborhoods: conditional cash transfer + after-school program vs unconditional CCT vs control. Cash alone improved healthy behaviors; combined arm's crime endpoints not in abstract - direct stipend+program architecture test exists but with health/economic endpoints, not crime.
entries.novelty_verdict: EXTENDED (closest analog to founder's stipend+program stack; crime endpoint unverified)

entries.authors: Magalhaes L, Ziebold M, Evans-Lacko S et al.
entries.title: Health, economic and social impacts of the Brazilian cash transfer program on the lives of its beneficiaries
entries.key_finding: Scoping review of Bolsa Familia effects (incl. crime/violence domains): family-scale cash transfers show broad social benefit; crime-specific evidence indirect.

entries.authors: Bonfim D, Alves F, Barreto M et al.
entries.title: Conditional cash transfer and mortality among interpersonal violence victims: A cohort study.
entries.key_finding: 100 Million Brazilian Cohort: Bolsa Familia participation associated with reduced mortality among interpersonal-violence victims - cash transfers as downstream protection on a violence-adjacent endpoint.
entries.effect_size: reduced mortality among victims (estimates in full text)

entries.authors: Sara R, Priyanka S
entries.title: Long-Term Effects of an Education Stipend Program on Domestic Violence: Evidence from Bangladesh
entries.key_finding: Secondary-school (aged-adolescent) stipend program vs later domestic-violence outcomes: the stipend-crime/violence evidence skew toward IPV/victimization and LMIC schooling programs, not US youth perpetration.
entries.novelty_verdict: EXTENDED (secondhand; stipend-violence channel is victimization-side, not offending-side)
entries.confidence: medium (secondhand: abstract not populated in loaded routes)

entries.authors: Muir J, Orlando C, Newton R et al.
entries.title: Impact of summer programmes on the outcomes of disadvantaged or 'at risk' young people: A systematic review
entries.key_finding: Campbell review of summer programmes for disadvantaged youth: employment-track summer programmes show promising offending outcomes, but NO age-band split of crime effects is reported - synthesis confirms evidence concentrated in summer jobs, weak elsewhere.
entries.novelty_verdict: EXTENDED (synthesis without the age-band verdict the founder wants)

entries.authors: Joseph PL, Jay J
entries.title: Summer Youth Employment Programs as a Structural Approach to Prevent Youth Violence: an Integrative Review
entries.key_finding: Integrative review positioning SYEPs as structural violence prevention: documents the mechanism stack (prosocial engagement, supervision, opportunity cost of violence, developmental opportunities) - but is organized by mechanism, NOT by age band.
entries.novelty_verdict: EXTENDED (the structural framing exists; the age-band differentiation was not found)

entries.authors: Schnippel K, Larson B, Jay J et al.
entries.title: Costs of Summer Youth Employment to Prevent Violence: an Analysis and Implementer's Tool
entries.key_finding: Cost-side analysis: places a per-participant, per-violence-event-averted price tag on SYEPs vs gun-homicide background (35% post-COVID rise) - the implementation ledger for the 13-18 jobs arc.
entries.effect_size: cost per participant/event in full text

entries.authors: Buil-Gil D, Birkbeck C, Enzmann D et al.
entries.title: Unstructured spare time as an international predictor of adolescent crime.
entries.key_finding: 58,425 13-to-17-year-olds in 21 countries: unstructured spare time is a robust correlate of self-reported adolescent offending - the time-occupation mechanism that both program arcs (under-13 after-school, 13-18 summer/jobs) sell, quantified in exactly the high-school years.

entries.authors: Durlak JA, Weissberg RP, Pachan M
entries.title: A meta-analysis of after-school programs that seek to promote personal and social skills in children and adolescents
entries.key_finding: Meta-analysis of 35 after-school programs: significant gains in self-perception, school bonding, positive behavior AND significant reductions in problem behaviors, when SAFE practices followed - the under-13-band canon, but endpoint is behavior ratings, not arrests/crime.
entries.effect_size: significant problem-behavior reductions (effect sizes in full text)

entries.authors: Durlak JA, Weissberg RP, Dymnicki AB et al.
entries.title: The Impact of Enhancing Students' Social and Emotional Learning: A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Universal Interventions
entries.key_finding: 213-program SEL meta-analysis (270,034 K-12 youth): improved skills, attitudes, behavior; school-based SEL canon for the younger band; again no crime/arrest endpoint.
entries.effect_size: mean effect sizes in full text
entries.confidence: high (secondhand: abstract not populated in loaded routes)

entries.authors: Gottfredson DC, Gerstenblith SA, Soule DA et al.
entries.title: Do after school programs reduce delinquency?
entries.key_finding: The direct delinquency test for after-school programs: effects on delinquency mostly null; benefits on delinquency-related attitudes/associations and (in combination with other programs) some reductions - the honest counterweight to 'after-school stops crime' in the younger band.

entries.authors: Rorie M, Gottfredson DC, Cross A
entries.title: Structure and deviancy training in after-school programs.
entries.key_finding: ~800 after-school programs: unstructured after-school settings can INCREASE antisocial behavior via deviancy training - the under-13 program-quality contingency that the founder's structured-tribe design must beat.
entries.novelty_verdict: VERIFIED (risk side: program design quality is decisive)

entries.authors: Thulin E, Lee E, Eisman A et al.
entries.title: Longitudinal effects of Youth Empowerment Solutions: Preventing youth aggression and increasing prosocial behavior
entries.key_finding: YES after-school program for MIDDLE-SCHOOL youth (the younger edge of the arc), longitudinal: reduced aggression, increased prosocial behavior - age-band-specific evidence but again behavioral endpoints, not crime.

entries.authors: Cid M
entries.title: Interventions Using Regular Activities to Engage High-Risk School-Age Youth: a Review of After-School Programs
entries.key_finding: Review of after-school activity programs against youth violence in Latin America/Caribbean: programs proliferate, causal evidence thin - LMIC replication of the under-13 after-school-crime evidence gap.

entries.authors: Trimmi K, Fouskas T, Yotsidi V et al.
entries.title: The Effectiveness of Life Skills-Based School Violence Prevention Programs in Secondary Education: A Systematic Review
entries.key_finding: Systematic review of life-skills school violence-prevention in SECONDARY education (13-18 band): promise claimed, effectiveness evidence in secondary education still limited - parallels the after-school gap on the school-side of the teen band.

entries.authors: Gal T, Lazar RL
entries.title: A Developmental Rights-Based Model for Minor-on-Minor Crime... Beyond the Adversarial Rivalry (Part 1)
entries.key_finding: Frameworks for age-appropriate handling of youth-perpetrated harm are being theorized (developmental/relational framing) but no empirically tested age-laddered program design was found anywhere in the sweep.
entries.novelty_verdict: EXTENDED (theory-side marker of the age-band gap)

entries.authors: Moffitt TE
entries.title: Adolescence-Limited and Life-Course-Persistent Antisocial Behavior: A Developmental Taxonomy
entries.key_finding: The two-group developmental taxonomy that justifies age-differentiated programming: adolescence-limited offenders (proximity to maturity + deviant-peer structure) are predicted malleable to situational/program levers (jobs, structured time), while life-course-persistent offenders are not.
entries.novelty_verdict: VERIFIED (theoretical basis: predicts the AGE-band split the founder assumes)
entries.confidence: high (secondhand: abstract not populated in loaded routes)

entries.authors: Jay J, Joseph PL, Goldstick JE
entries.title: Age-Specific Trends in Pediatric and Adult Firearm Homicide After the Onset of the COVID-19 Pandemic
entries.key_finding: Pediatric vs adult firearm-homicide trends diverge post-COVID - youth-band-specific violence dynamics are empirically real and measurable, a data precondition for a band-differentiated program model.
entries.confidence: high (secondhand: abstract not populated in loaded routes)

entries.authors: Vahora J, Dove E et al.
entries.title: Navigating Health Equity Through Mobility Justice: Youth of Color Organizing for Transportation Equity
entries.key_finding: Youth-of-color mobility-justice organizing: transportation access documented as a structurally rationed determinant for youth participation in programs/services - framing literature only; NO experimental test of transportation provision as a program-funding input on participation or crime.
entries.novelty_verdict: EXTENDED (frame exists) / near-GAP on causal tests

entries.authors: Hanson KG, Satchell AK, Skinner ML, Eddy JM
entries.title: Implementing a professional youth mentoring program during times of crisis: lessons from the global pandemic
entries.key_finding: Friends of the Children professional mentoring (youth avg age 12.5, majority Black): pandemic disruptions of transportation/in-person access forced engagement redesign - the closest retrieved analog to 'transportation as a program-continuity input' for the under-13 band.

entries.authors: Thakuriah (Vonu) P, Persky J
entries.title: Costs and benefits of employment transportation for low-wage workers: An assessment of job access public transportation
entries.key_finding: Adult analog: job-access transportation for low-wage workers costed with employment benefits - the transportation-funding-plate mechanism exists in employment economics for adults but was NOT found transplanted to youth-program participation or crime.
entries.confidence: high (secondhand: abstract not populated in loaded routes)

summary: Novelty verdict summary (SCAN-12, age-ladder): The 13-18 band is the VERIFIED side: summer youth employment is the best-causalized youth anti-crime intervention in the world - Heller 2014 Science RCT (1,634 youth, violent-crime arrests -43% over 55 wks) plus NYC lotteries (Kessler 2021 crime; Leos-Urbel 2014 attendance; Modestino & Paulsen 2019 Boston), a risk-tail extension (READI 2024: null primary index but ~1/3 fewer shooting/homicide arrests), scale/unpacking notes (Bertrand & Repka 2015), integrative review (Joseph & Jay 2026) and a cost tool (Schnippel 2023). The stipend+program stack has one direct test (Stacy 2023 RCT, young men 14-17) but with health/economic endpoints, not crime; cash-transfer crime evidence skews to family-scale international programs and victimization-side outcomes (Bolsa Familia: Magalhaes 2024, Bonfim 2026; Bangladesh education stipend 2023). The UNDER-13 band is behavior-verified but crime-evidence-thin: Durlak metas (2010 after-school; 2011 SEL) show problem-behavior reductions with NO arrest/crime endpoint; the one direct delinquency test (Gottfredson 2004) is null-to-small; deviancy-training counter-mechanism (Rorie 2011) means unstructured under-13 programming can backfire; unstructured spare time is a verified cross-national correlate of offending at ages 13-17 (Buil-Gil 2026). Age-structure theory is on the founder's side: Moffitt's taxonomy predicts situational levers (structured time, jobs) work best on the adolescence-limited group, i.e., the 13-18 band is theory-predicted responsive - but NOT ONE retrieved study explicitly compares program-vs-crime effect sizes across two age bands in a single design, and Muir 2024 (Campbell) synthesizes summer programs without a band split. TRANSPORTATION is the most NOVEL lever: the retrieved literature contains mobility-justice framing (Vahora 2023), a continuity case in mentoring (Hanson 2026), and an adult job-access-transit cost-benefit analog (Thakuriah & Persky 2013) - but no causal study of transportation provision as a youth-program input for participation, attendance, or crime anywhere in the sweep. => (a) 13-18 summer-jobs-crime effect = VERIFIED; (b) under-13 programs-behavior = VERIFIED, under-13 programs-crime = GAP; (c) stipend-on-crime for youth = GAP (adjacent RCT exists with wrong endpoints); (d) age-band-differentiated effect comparison = NOVEL-ANGLE (leaning GAP); (e) transportation-as-program-funding-plate on crime = NOVEL-ANGLE / near-GAP (strongest novelty in the stack).
